question: A hospital has three scans from each patient. Which train/test split best avoids leakage when evaluating a disease-classification model?
options: Keep every scan from the same patient together in either training or the held-out test partition
Place the original scan in testing and augmented variants in training to measure robustness under augmentation
Randomize scans independently and then adjust the chosen split based on which gives the highest test score
Balance the number of scans per partition, even if some patients contribute images to both partitions
explanation: Patient-level separation prevents a model from exploiting highly similar images from one patient in both training and testing. Random image-level splits can inflate reported generalization.
source: L8 Medicine slides 29-42 (medical datasets, splitting, data processing) and 49-59 (model development and evaluation).

question: A classifier detects no positive cases in a cohort with 90 negatives and 10 positives. It calls everyone negative. What are accuracy and positive-class sensitivity?
explanation: Ninety of 100 labels are correct, so accuracy is 90%. It finds zero of ten positives, so sensitivity is zero. This is why class prevalence and clinically relevant error costs matter.
source: L8 Medicine slides 40-56 (data quality, model selection and performance); instructional example.

question: For a segmentation model, the predicted tumor has 80 positive voxels, ground truth has 100, and overlap contains 60. What is the Dice similarity coefficient?
explanation: Dice = 2|P ∩ G|/(|P|+|G|)=120/180≈0.667. Raw accuracy over predominantly background voxels is not an adequate substitute for overlap evaluation.
source: L8 Medicine slides 13-18 (segmentation applications) and 50-58 (model evaluation); instructional Dice calculation.

question: A PET image and a CT image from one patient are combined for prediction. What is the central data-management challenge?
options: Align the modalities spatially and reconcile acquisition metadata and patient/study identifiers
Average image intensities across modalities, because registration is unnecessary for scans of the same patient
Use the CT acquisition timestamp alone to align every PET voxel, irrespective of scanner geometry
Convert both modalities into identical arrays, which also guarantees matching anatomical coordinates and labels
explanation: Multimodal learning can combine complementary information, but registration/alignment, metadata and identity consistency are required. Different modalities are not automatically in a shared coordinate system.
source: L8 Medicine slides 13-17 and 40-47 (multimodal medical data and variability).

question: A lab wants to reproduce a tumor segmentation result after changing labels and preprocessing code. Which artifact set is most useful?
options: The trained weights and final segmentation score, since the original image and annotation versions can be inferred
Exact images, annotations, split definitions, preprocessing code and versions, plus model and training metadata
The predicted masks and patient identifiers, since transformations can be reconstructed from output geometries
The model architecture and inference logs, without storing dataset/annotation versions or training configuration
explanation: Data and model lineage connects inputs, preprocessing, annotations, code and checkpoints. A metric alone cannot explain or reproduce a result when the data or pipeline changes.
source: L8 Medicine slides 47-48 and 59-70 (data saved, experimentation and model management).
